examples: His theory is difficult to understand even for experts.
I forgot my wallet, so I don't even have money to buy water.
I'm so busy that I can't even find time to talk with my family.
With an old PC, even sending and receiving email is a struggle.
That fact was not known even to the people involved.
fields.explain:
Often used with ～ない/難しい/不足する to strengthen the negative nuance.
Emphatic and formal; also common in ads and headlines that aim for a strong impression.
Avoid overusing it in casual conversation, as it sounds stiff.

“～にすら/～すら” = “even …”. Stronger than “～さえ”; usually used with negative sentences or difficulties to emphasize surprise, or a degree of badness/harshness beyond expectations.
• Choose “にすら” when the function of “に” must be kept: recipient, place, point in time.
• It emphasizes a minimal example, from which it follows that the other cases are naturally true as well.
• Used a lot in written language, newspapers and speeches; in spoken language, “さえ” is more natural.
fields.notes:
• The closer “すら” is placed to the element being emphasized, the stronger the effect: 「彼にすらできない」 vs 「彼はすらできない」.
• With abstract verbs: 想像すらしなかった／予想すらしなかった → “did not even imagine”.
• In polite style: 説明は専門家ですら難解です。
mistakes: Using “にすら” in the wrong place: × 水にすらない → 〇 水すらない.
Confusing it with “さえ”: exam questions test the nuance; “すら” = more formal/stronger.
Forgetting to nominalize when attaching it to a verb: × 行くすらできない → 〇 行くことすらできない.

rows: <ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>どころか、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
More polite; usually in serious writing
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>ですら<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>いた。

fields.meaning: Whenever… / every time…; both when ~ and when ~
examples: Whatever I see or hear of it, I can only bow my head to his hard work.
Whether happy or sad, she writes it down in her diary.
Whenever I look at photos, I remember my childhood.
Stop complaining about every little thing, rain or wind.
Every time I hear foreign news, it makes me think about how precious peace is.
I tend to rely on him for everything.
fields.explain:
When using the paired form, the two elements before につけ should be balanced (verbs/adjectives of the same type, or an opposing pair).
The second clause usually expresses emotions, evaluations or general habits; avoid using it with commands or intentions.
The single form Vる + につけ emphasizes that “each time/on every occasion one meets that situation” an emotional reaction arises.
Somewhat formal style; used a lot in writing, speeches and essays.

• Paired form: “whenever A …, whenever B …” → the result/emotion in the second clause is the same.
• Single form: “every time V, …”, close to ～たびに but usually tied to emotions, recollections and evaluations.
• The nuance leans toward emotion, lament and reflection; it does not suit concrete commands/intentions.
• Often combines with verbs of emotion/recollection: 思い出す, 感心する, 心が痛む, 考えさせられる, 胸が熱くなる.
fields.notes:
• Typical pairs: 見るにつけ聞くにつけ／読むにつけ書くにつけ／うれしいにつけ悲しいにつけ.
• “何事につけ” means “in everything …” and is very common in written language.
• This pattern suits general, repeated topics; avoid using it for single events that happen only once in the future.
mistakes: Using a command/volition after ～につけ: unnatural. Incorrect example: “見るにつけ、来てください”。
Combining two unbalanced parts: “見るにつけ悲しいにつけ” (verb + adjective) is incorrect; they should be of the same type.
Confusing it with ～につれて: ～につけ does not express gradual change over time.
Using it for a single event: “明日会うにつけ、報告する” does not fit; use ～たら/～とき instead.

rows: Broader meaning, also used for intentional actions; ～につけ leans toward emotion/evaluation.
<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るたびに<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す。
Almost synonymous with the single form of ～につけ; につけて has a written-language nuance.
<ruby>故郷<rt>こきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>すことがあるにつけて…
Expresses gradual change; does not mean “every time”.
<ruby>年<rt>とし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>るにつれて<ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きになる。
Refers to a special, one-time point in time; differs from the repetitive nature of ～につけ.
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>にあたって<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>する。

examples: Support measures that match the actual situation are needed.
We created a manual suited to the actual worksite.
We will carry out a review in line with the actual conditions.
The explanation must be faithful to the facts.
We provide services that meet local needs.
We follow procedures in accordance with laws and regulations.
fields.explain:
Used with nouns of circumstance: 実情・現場・実態・事実・ニーズ・状況・要件…
Context of work/policy/documents: emphasizes practical suitability.
Note the difference between the two kanji: 即 (suited to the situation) vs 則 (following rules).

• “～に即した” describes the following noun as suited to, matching the context/circumstances/needs stated in N.
• The focus is on being “practical/realistic/timely” rather than merely “following rules”.
• “～に則した” emphasizes compliance with rules, laws and standards (norms).
fields.notes:
• Base verbs: 即する（そくする）/ 則する（そくする）. They are pronounced the same, so the kanji are easily confused.
• In legal/normative documents, prefer “則”. In practical/situational contexts, use “即”.
• “即した” is a fixed attributive form (even though it is past), functioning like an adjective to modify the following noun.
mistakes: Wrong kanji: writing “法令に即した” when the meaning is “in accordance with the law” → it should be “法令に則した”.
Using “に基づく” when you want to say “suited to the situation” → use “に即した”.
Confusing it with “に沿った”: “現場に沿った” is unnatural; it should be “現場に即した”.
JLPT: choose between 即/則 based on the context, “actual circumstances” vs “norms”.

rows: Practical, according to the specific circumstances.
<ruby>現場<rt>げんば</rt></ruby>に<ruby>即<rt>そく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>規定<rt>きてい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>則<rt>そく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>運用<rt>うんよう</rt></ruby>。
Follows a guideline/plan already laid out.
<ruby>方針<rt>ほうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>沿<rt>そ</rt></ruby>った<ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>。
Used when there is clear data/reasons.
データに<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいた<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>踏<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>まえた<ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>。

examples: The footage of the accident is so gruesome that it's unbearable to watch.
The vulgar remarks went on, with words too offensive to listen to.
This novel is so clumsily written that it isn't worth reading.
I am deeply grateful for your kindness.
This scandal is truly most regrettable.
fields.explain:
V of the senses/perception: 見る・聞く・読む・鑑賞する・直視する + に堪えない.
Nouns of emotion: 感謝・喜び・同情・憤り・遺憾 + に堪えない (a standard expression in official documents).
The tone is strong, so consider the level of politeness and your relationship with the listener when using it.

• Unbearable/heartbreaking: so terrible, miserable or vulgar that one “cannot bear to watch/listen/read”.
• Not worth V-ing: quality so poor that it is not worth watching/reading… (a harsh evaluation).
• Emphasizes strong emotion: with nouns of emotion: 感謝/喜び/同情/遺憾 + に堪えない = “extremely …”.
• Style: written language, formal; in the negative sense with V, it is often seen in commentary/criticism.
fields.notes:
• In terms of form, with V it is usually V-る + に堪えない (unlike some materials that give V-ます語幹 + に堪えない; the common usage is V-る, as in 見るに堪えない).
• “に堪えない” with nouns of emotion has a formal, official-document nuance and is often found in speeches and press statements.
• In art criticism, “鑑賞に堪えない” emphasizes poor aesthetic value.
mistakes: Using it with an unsuitable verb (e.g. 操作するに堪えない sounds odd). Prefer verbs of perception/reception.
Confusing the positive nuance of “感謝に堪えない” with the negative one of “見るに堪えない”. Same form, but opposite nuances.
Confusing “に堪えない” with “に足りない/に値しない” (different emotional degree and scope of use).

rows: Worth/good enough to V; able to withstand
Positive opposite; used for works/performance that “meet the standard”.
<ruby>鑑賞<rt>かんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える<ruby>作品<rt>さくひん</rt></ruby>。
Similar meaning; “<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” are almost interchangeable in this pattern.
～に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>しない／<ruby>足<rt>た</rt></ruby>りない
A more rational evaluation; less strong emotional nuance.
<ruby>一読<rt>いちどく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>しない。

examples: This movie is well made enough to be worth watching.
Although it's a paper by a newcomer, its content is worth reading.
This data can withstand rigorous verification.
It is designed to withstand continuous outdoor use.
We refined it into a theory that can stand up to criticism.
fields.explain:
Used a lot in professional evaluations: art, academia, engineering.
The point is “meeting the standard/having value”, not excessive praise.
Unlike “いい/素晴らしい”, this pattern evaluates whether objective criteria are met.

• Worth/good enough to V: a work/product is of sufficient quality to be watched/read/listened to/evaluated.
• Able to withstand/meet: can withstand continuous use, verification, criticism…
• Style: written language, formal, often a professional/technical evaluation.
fields.notes:
• V-ます語幹 + に堪える is the natural form: 読む→読みに堪える, 見る→見るに堪える (both 読み/見る are found; with 見る/聞く, the V-る form is also common in set phrases).
• In technical standards, common combinations: 実用・耐久・検証・批判 + に堪える.
• In art criticism: 鑑賞に堪える作品／名品.
mistakes: Wrong verb form: V-ます語幹 is needed (読みに堪える); avoid 読むに堪える in technical evaluations; however, with 見る・聞く in art commentary, “見るに堪える” is still natural.
Confusing the nuance of “meeting an objective standard” with emotional praise; the JLPT often tests this difference.
Confusing “堪える” with “耐える”: both are correct in many cases, but “堪える” leans toward evaluation/value, while “耐える” leans toward physical endurance.

rows: Negative opposite; used when quality is bad or something is painful.
Close synonym, leans toward rational evaluation; more widely used.
<ruby>一見<rt>いっけん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>する。
“<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える” and “<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” are close in meaning; “<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” is more formal/written.
<ruby>長時間<rt>ちょうじかん</rt></ruby><ruby>使用<rt>しよう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える。

examples: We're childhood friends, so he's practically family to me.
At this price, it's practically free.
They're three points behind after the first half, so they've as good as lost.
I haven't heard back from her for a whole week. I've as good as been dumped.
Since nobody takes care of it, that house is practically a ruin.
This mistake is as good as a fatal blow for the company.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize a degree of near equivalence, often with emotion (surprise, lament, confident judgment).
Often appears with nouns expressing extremes: 無一文, タダ, 死, 廃墟, 失業, 致命傷, … to add weight.
In formal writing, it can be replaced with ～に等しい (more serious and objective).
Before “も同然だ” there is usually N or Vた; adjectives are rare and are usually converted to N (例:貧乏も同然だ).
Not used when the equivalence is weak; in that case choose 「ようなものだ／と言ってもいい」.

• States near-complete equivalence between A and B: AはBも同然だ = A is practically B.
• With Vた: emphasizes that “the result can be considered to have happened”, even if in reality it has not fully happened (e.g. 負けたも同然だ = a sure loss/as good as lost).
• Highly subjective: the speaker judges based on common sense, experience or emotion.
• Can carry an exaggerating nuance to persuade or complain (死んだも同然だ = as good as dead).
fields.notes:
• “同然” is a Sino-Japanese noun meaning “exactly the same/natural”; it can also be used on its own in written language: 同然の扱い.
• With Vた, the sense “as good as already…” easily sounds pessimistic or like a premature verdict; mind the context so it does not sound blunt.
• Combines with exaggerating quantity words: ゼロも同然, 無意味も同然, 無駄も同然 for stronger emphasis.
• In newspaper headlines: 「値上げは増税も同然」 is used to make a strong argument. explain: Means that although it is not actually the case, the state is almost like that. Expressive and subjective. ⏐ examples: 1. この車は中古車といっても新品（も）同然だ。
This car may be used, but it's just like new.
2. 彼の財産はないも同然だ。
He has practically no assets.
mistakes: Wrong combination with adjectives: × 寒いも同然だ → should be changed to 名詞化: × 寒さも同然だ → use another pattern, “寒いようなものだ”.
Confusing it with ～に違いない: “も同然だ” is a comparison of degree, not a confident conjecture.
Using it when the equivalence is weak → unnatural. Choose ～ようなものだ/～と言ってもいい instead.
JLPT: easily confused with ～に等しい (formal) and ～同様だ (emphasizes general similarity). Distinguish the strong subjective nuance of “も同然”.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>同然<rt>どうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>等<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>しないのと<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じようなものだ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>天才<rt>てんさい</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってもいい。
それは<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>と<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じだ。

examples: This bridge is designed to withstand major earthquakes.
He endured pain for many years and continued his research.
Even reread today, this novel is a masterpiece well worth reading.
The noise is so bad that this recording is simply not worth listening to.
Wartime testimonies are valuable enough to be cited as historical sources.
fields.explain:
Meaning 1 has a nuance of resilience/endurance; the subject is usually a person/thing subjected to an impact.
Meaning 2 has a nuance of evaluating quality/value. Used in criticism, reports and formal written language.
「～に耐えるN」 usually comes before a noun: 読むに耐える内容・使用に耐える強度。
The negative 「～に耐えない」 emphasizes “unacceptable/not worth…”, with a strong nuance.

• Meaning 1: To endure/resist an unpleasant or harsh impact (physical/mental): 痛み・寒さ・重圧・地震 など。
• Meaning 2: Valuable enough for an act of appreciation/evaluation: 見る・読む・鑑賞・批判・使用 など。「～に耐えるN」 = N good enough to …
• Formality: neutral → formal (when written with 堪). Meaning 2 is often used in written language/academic evaluation and criticism.
• Verb restrictions for meaning 2: usually used with verbs of perception/evaluation (見る・読む・鑑賞する・使用する…). With ordinary verbs it can sound forced.
fields.notes:
• Kanji: 耐える・堪える. For the meaning “worth…”, 堪える is usually used in formal writing.
• Typical collocations (meaning 2): 観賞/鑑賞・見る・読む・批判・引用・使用 + に耐える。
• Avoid overusing it with everyday action verbs (食べるに耐える…): it sounds forced. Use it with activities of evaluation/appreciation.
• In engineering: 耐震・耐熱・耐水 are common prefixes meaning “resistant to …”.
mistakes: Mixing up meanings: using ～に耐える to say “easy to do” → incorrect. It means “can withstand/worth”, not “easy”.
Using it with an unsuitable verb: 食べるに耐える sounds unnatural. Prefer verbs of appreciation/evaluation.
Forgetting the strong nuance of ～に耐えない: using it in casual speech can be too harsh.
JLPT N1: Distinguish ～に耐える vs ～に耐えかねる vs ～に堪えない in contexts of evaluation/criticism.

rows: <ruby>鑑賞<rt>かんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>
<ruby>直視<rt>ちょくし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>えない<ruby>光景<rt>こうけい</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes going beyond the limit of endurance
<ruby>屈辱<rt>くつじょく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>えかねて<ruby>退職<rt>たいしょく</rt></ruby>した
Describes general properties, little evaluative “worth” nuance
<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>素材<rt>そざい</rt></ruby>

examples: After several rounds of negotiations, an agreement was finally reached.
The infection spread throughout the body and, sadly, resulted in death.
After a series of defects, shipments of the product ended up being halted.
Years of research bore fruit, and the technology reached practical use.
Leaving the problem unaddressed was the biggest factor that led to the loss of trust.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the final result while implying a process that led there.
Formal/objective style: reports, administrative documents, news.
The subject is usually an organization/event; the speaker keeps their own feelings at a distance.
With personal actions, it is used when one wants to sound objective: 私的な事情により辞職 に至った。

• Expresses a process of accumulation/developments and the final outcome “reached/arrived at”.
• Often used in written language, news and reports. Often goes with negative results (死亡・中止・破綻) but can also be neutral/positive (合意・実用化・採用)。
• Objective nuance, describing a result after many factors/developments; avoid using it for the speaker's direct emotions.
fields.notes:
• 「至る」 is a formal verb meaning “to arrive at, to reach”. The past form 「至った」 confirms a result that has already happened.
• Often accompanied by a nominalized cause phrase: ～が原因で／～の結果、～に至った。
• Newspaper headlines often shorten it to the present: 死亡に至る、合意に至る（a reporting sense, not future).
mistakes: Using it for direct personal emotions → unnatural: ×うれしくて笑うに至った → just use: 笑うようになった。
Confusing it with 「～に至るまで」 (scope) → it does not express a result.
Losing the formal nuance: in casual conversation, 「結局～になった」 is more natural.
JLPT N1: Recognize it when used with nouns of serious outcomes (死亡・破綻) and in report style.

rows: Emphasizes the outcome after a process
<ruby>解散<rt>かいさん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>った
Not a “result”, but an extension of scope
<ruby>末端<rt>まったん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>るまで<ruby>検査<rt>けんさ</rt></ruby>
When it came to… / only when…
States the point in time when something arose
<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>拡大<rt>かくだい</rt></ruby>するに<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>って<ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>
Focuses on a chain of efforts→result; more emotional
<ruby>協議<rt>きょうぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>末<rt>すえ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>
